Shook up
SHOOK UP
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
Shook up (nonstandard for shaken up) meant upset or agitated; Elvis Presley’s 1957 number-one hit "All Shook Up," written by Otis Blackwell, made it the phrase of the year, though there it meant the trembling of a young man in love. The participle shook for shaken is old and regional; shake is Old English sceacan.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1957 every teenager in America was singing that he was all shook up, and the phrase stuck for anything that rattled you: bad news, a near miss on the highway, a scare at the doctor’s office. "She was pretty shook up after the accident." Scripture knows the feeling well, and it knows the cure. The Psalmist pictured the whole world shaking and still sang, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble" (Psa 46:1). David, hunted by enemies, said, "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved" (Psa 62:2). When the disciples were shook up in a storm on the lake, the Lord Jesus "rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm" (Mar 4:39). And to frightened men on the night before His death He said, "Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid" (Joh 14:27). Grandchildren, you will be shook up many times in this life, and that is no sin. The question is where you run when the ground moves. Everything in this world can be shaken, but believers are "receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved" (Heb 12:28). Run to the King of that kingdom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (made famous by a 1957 hit song) for upset or rattled — a common trouble with an old cure: He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved (Psa 62:2).

SHOOK UP, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; from nonstandard shook for shaken; "All Shook Up," 1957) Upset, agitated, rattled; in the song, trembling with love. "Mom was all shook up after the fender-bender."

Decode for families: rattled; the Lord says, Peace, be still.

Key Scripture

Psa 46:1 — "To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."

Psa 62:2 — "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved."

Mar 4:39 — "And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm."

Joh 14:27 — "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."

Heb 12:28 — "Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:"

Modern Corruption

A plain, honest phrase for being upset, with nothing sinful in it; the only question is where the shaken heart runs.

expand to see more

Being shook up is not a sin. The Lord Jesus Himself was troubled in spirit, and the Psalms are full of men whose hearts were shaken. The slang names a real human experience honestly.

If there is anything to watch, it is the song’s use, which made romantic feeling into a kind of helpless fever. Feeling is not the master of a Christian; Christ is. Whether the shaking comes from fear or from infatuation, the believer brings it to the One who calms storms.

Old English sceacan (to shake) → shaken, nonstandard shook → 1950s shook up (upset).
